issues.description: The abstract, introduction, and discussion repeatedly describe the sample as a 'national probability sample' and 'nationally representative sample,' yet the Methods section explicitly states participants were recruited 'through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington,' with a mean age of 19.42 years and N=374. These two descriptions are mutually incompatible. A university introductory psychology pool is a convenience sample of undergraduates, not a national probability sample. The entire comparative narrative of the paper—distinguishing this study from Stanley et al.'s student sample—collapses if this sample is also a student pool. This contradiction undermines the central framing and all generalizability claims.
issues.quote: We recruited participants through the introductory psychology participant pool at Victoria University of Wellington... the average age was 19 years at Time 1 (2009; M = 19.42, SD = 2.31) and 68% were female.

issues.description: The Strengths and Limitations section asserts 'Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population.' This claim is not supportable given the methods as described (intro psych pool, M age=19, N=374, 68% female, 86% Pākehā). Even if the sample were NZAVS data (referenced elsewhere in the paper), claiming high generalizability to New Zealand without reporting sampling weights or comparing demographic profiles to census data is insufficient. The demographic composition (near-universal youth, majority female) is not representative of the New Zealand adult population.
issues.quote: Our research uses a nationally representative sample, meaning that our results are highly generalisable, at least to the New Zealand population.

issues.description: The paper's title, abstract, current study section, results, and discussion consistently describe the outcome variable as 'willingness to change behaviour to protect the environment' or 'willingness to make sacrifices for the environment.' However, the Measures section describes the scale as measuring 'concern about environmental problems,' with items about how concerned participants are and whether environmental problems are exaggerated—both attitude/perception items, not behavioral intention items. These are conceptually distinct constructs. Willingness to act requires behavioral intention items; concern is an affective/cognitive appraisal. The WILL variable label in Table 1 is never justified by the described items. This mismatch means all conclusions about behavioral change are not supported by the operationalization.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as participants' concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley's [28] environmental concern scale, 'How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?' and 'To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?'

issues.description: The reported unstandardized coefficient, standard error, and confidence interval for the RWA-to-WILL cross-lagged path are internally inconsistent. With B = -.02 and SE = .01, the 95% CI should be approximately [-.04, .00], not [-.05, -.01] as reported. If the CI is [-.05, -.01], the implied SE is approximately .01, which could marginally produce this range only under asymmetric bootstrapping—but no asymmetric CI method is described. Furthermore, the upper bound of -.01 (not -.00) means the CI does not include zero, which would make the effect significant, but under a standard calculation with B=-.02 and SE=.01 the interval barely excludes zero. The inconsistency suggests either B, SE, or the CI is incorrectly transcribed, undermining confidence in reported significance.

Throughout the Results section, the variability of regression coefficients is labeled 'SD' (standard deviation), but the appropriate statistic is 'SE' (standard error). Standard deviations describe dispersion of a distribution of scores; standard errors describe precision of a parameter estimate. This is a systematic terminology error across all coefficient reports (e.g., 'B = -.11, SD = .01'; 'B = -.04, SD = .002'). While the values themselves may be standard errors, mislabeling them as standard deviations makes the results uninterpretable and constitutes a reporting error.
issues.quote: SDO was a stronger predictor of change in environmental sacrifice (B = -.11, SD = .01, p < .001, 95% CI [-.13, -.09]) than RWA (B = -.02, SD = .01, p = .001, 95% CI [-.05, -.01])

issues.description: The authors conduct a chi-square model comparison test to determine whether SDO is a statistically stronger predictor of environmentalism than RWA. This test yields χ²(1) = 2.34, p = .126—a non-significant result indicating the two paths cannot be statistically distinguished. Despite this, the authors conclude 'SDO is a stronger predictor of change in willingness to sacrifice for the environment than RWA in our sample' and later describe SDO as a 'significantly stronger prospective predictor.' The null hypothesis (paths are equal) was not rejected. Interpreting raw coefficient differences as meaningful when the formal test is non-significant is a logical error that overstates the reliability of this key finding.
issues.quote: We found that our original model provides comparable fit to the data χ2(1) = 2.34, p = .126, but based on the pattern of unstandardized coefficients we interpret SDO as a stronger predictor of change in willingness to sacrifice for the environment than RWA in our sample.

issues.description: The reported chi-square value for comparing the bidirectional paths between SDO and RWA is χ²(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001. A chi-square value of over 15,000 for a 1 degree-of-freedom test comparing two constrained paths within a single structural model is extraordinarily implausible. Chi-square difference tests in SEM comparing path equality constraints typically produce values in the range of single digits to low hundreds. A value of this magnitude suggests either a computational or transcription error. Given that this finding is discussed substantively ('RWA predicts SDO but SDO does not predict RWA'), an error here would materially affect the interpretation.
issues.quote: These lagged effects were also statistically different (χ2(1) = 15,389.13, p < .001), a finding we explore more fully in the Discussion.

issues.description: The RMSEA confidence interval is reported as 90% CI [.025, .026]—a width of only .001. RMSEA confidence intervals in structural equation models with hundreds of degrees of freedom are never this narrow. For reference, even models with very large N and stable solutions routinely produce RMSEA CIs spanning .01 to .05 or more. This appears to be a reporting error, possibly a truncation of the actual interval (e.g., [.025, .036] or [.025, .026] where the second digit is wrong). Because RMSEA is a primary index for evaluating model fit in this study, this error affects the ability of readers to evaluate the adequacy of the model.
issues.quote: those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03, 90% CI [.025, .026], SRMR = .07)

issues.description: The authors report CFI = .86, which falls below widely accepted thresholds for adequate model fit (CFI ≥ .90 is commonly required; ≥ .95 preferred). The rationale for accepting the model despite suboptimal CFI—that CFI is 'affected by model complexity'—is insufficient. CFI was specifically designed to be relatively insensitive to sample size and model complexity compared to the chi-square test. Accepting a model with CFI = .86 without exploring potential sources of misfit (e.g., modification indices, alternative parameterizations) or conducting sensitivity analyses means the reported cross-lagged parameters may be biased by an inadequately fitting model.
issues.quote: Overall, model fit was poorer for those indices affected by model complexity (e.g. χ2(2279) = 36511.73, p < .001, CFI = .86), however those less influenced by complexity pointed to good fit (RMSEA = .03, 90% CI [.025, .026], SRMR = .07), therefore the model was accepted.

issues.description: The paper repeatedly uses causal language throughout ('causal pathway,' 'causal effect,' 'having a causal effect on environmental attitudes,' 'being foundational for these attitudes') to describe findings from a cross-lagged panel model (CLPM). CLPMs do not establish causation; they show that one variable predicts another's change while controlling for prior levels, but this is consistent with many causal and non-causal explanations, including unmeasured common causes, regression to the mean, and spurious associations due to trait-level confounding. The authors do briefly mention alternative explanations but then continue using causal language. Moreover, CLPMs in particular have been critiqued (e.g., Hamaker et al., 2015) for confounding within-person and between-person effects, which is not acknowledged.
issues.quote: These results suggest that there is a causal pathway from ideological attitudes to environmentalism... With our findings of a temporal connection between SDO and environmentalism, this strengthens our confidence in SDO having a causal effect on environmental attitudes, and perhaps even being foundational for these attitudes.

issues.description: The paper uses listwise deletion for a five-year longitudinal study across five time points and reports N=374. However, the initial sample size at Time 1, retention at each subsequent wave, and total attrition across the study are never reported. In a five-wave student panel study, attrition is typically substantial, and listwise deletion (complete case analysis) produces biased estimates when data are missing not completely at random (MCAR). Students who drop out may systematically differ in SDO, RWA, or environmentalism. Without reporting attrition rates and testing for differential dropout, readers cannot assess whether the analyzed sample is representative even of the original sample, let alone the broader population.
issues.quote: Analyses were conducted using listwise deletion.

issues.description: The primary outcome variable (WILL) is inadequately described. Only two items are reported for the environmentalism measure (concern and exaggeration items), and no total number of items is stated. The scale's psychometric properties beyond reliability are absent. Critically, the WILL abbreviation implies 'willingness' throughout the paper, but the described items measure concern and denial, not behavioral willingness. No information is given about how items were scored (direction of the exaggeration item is reversed but this is not discussed), how they were combined, or whether a confirmatory factor model was applied. This prevents replication and adequate evaluation.
issues.quote: Environmentalism was measured as participants' concern about environmental problems. These items were modelled from Liu and Sibley's [28] environmental concern scale, 'How concerned are you about the current state of the natural environment?' and 'To what extent do you think environmental problems have been exaggerated?'.

issues.description: The paper imposes a stationary (time-invariant) cross-lagged model, treating all parameters as equal across time points. However, this approach requires first establishing measurement invariance—that the items measure the same construct with the same factor loadings and intercepts at each wave. The paper reports no configural, metric, or scalar invariance tests. Moreover, the RWA scale has one fewer item at Time 2, creating an explicit non-equivalence in measurement across waves. Without invariance testing, the assumption of equal parameters across time is unfounded, and cross-lagged estimates may be confounded by changes in measurement rather than reflecting genuine construct change.
issues.quote: The item 'Some of the best people in our country are those who are challenging our government, criticizing religion, and ignoring the "normal way" things are supposed to be done', was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points.

issues.description: The Methods section states 'we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings,' but the Figure 1 caption states 'All meet our accepted threshold for significance of p < .01 unless otherwise noted.' These are inconsistent thresholds. If the figure uses p < .01 as the threshold, some paths shown as significant in the figure may not meet the p < .05 threshold declared in the methods (or vice versa). This inconsistency undermines confidence in which findings are being claimed as significant and whether the stated decision rule was consistently applied.
issues.quote: Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings. [...] All meet our accepted threshold for significance of p < .01 unless otherwise noted.

issues.description: The same methodological step is described twice in the Data Analysis section using nearly identical language: the constraint of cross-lagged associations to equality across measurement points appears as both the first and final sentence of the constraint description. This verbatim repetition ('We started by constraining the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point' and 'Finally, we constrained the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point') suggests either a copy-paste error or that additional constraints intended to appear between these sentences were inadvertently deleted, leaving the method description incomplete or inaccurate.
issues.quote: We started by constraining the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point... Finally, we constrained the cross-lagged associations between the constructs to be the same in each measurement point.

issues.description: Table 1 reports '95% confidence intervals based on 1000 iterations' for descriptive statistics and correlations. This implies bootstrapped confidence intervals, but the Data Analysis section makes no mention of bootstrapping as a method for any analyses. The software used for bootstrapping, the bootstrapping procedure, and whether the same approach was applied to path coefficients are all unspecified. The confidence intervals for cross-lagged paths in the Results (e.g., '[-.13, -.09]') do not specify whether they are bootstrapped or model-based. This inconsistency in CI computation methods is not explained.
issues.quote: Numbers in square brackets represent 95% confidence intervals based on 1000 iterations.

issues.description: The authors justify using p < .05 (rather than a more stringent threshold) on the grounds of 'the large sample size of this dataset,' yet N=374 is not a large sample—particularly for a five-wave, three-construct cross-lagged panel model with numerous free parameters. In SEM with many parameters, N=374 may produce underpowered tests for some effects and is far below the thousands of observations typical of studies where size-based threshold corrections are warranted. This mischaracterization may lead readers to believe the sample provides more statistical precision than it does. The justification is also internally contradictory: large samples typically warrant stricter thresholds (e.g., p < .01) to avoid capitalizing on chance, not more lenient ones.
issues.quote: Because of the large sample size of this dataset, we adopted a significance threshold of p < .05 to indicate significance of findings.

issues.description: The Methods section states that 'Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website.' Outsourcing fundamental methodological details—retention rates, full demographic breakdowns, sampling procedure—to an external website violates reporting standards. Peer reviewers and readers cannot adequately evaluate the study's validity, potential for selection bias, or representativeness without this information in the manuscript itself. Additionally, external website content may change or become unavailable, compromising replicability.
issues.quote: Full details about the sample, including the procedure, retention, and demographics of participants, are available on the NZAVS website.

issues.description: The study involves a longitudinal dataset spanning five years with multiple analytical choices (model constraints, variable selection, significance thresholds, handling of missing RWA item, deletion strategy). No pre-registration is mentioned, and there is no disclosure of alternative models considered or sensitivity analyses conducted. Given that several analytical decisions are consequential for the main findings (e.g., choice of stationary versus non-stationary model, listwise versus multiple imputation, which items to retain for RWA at T2), the absence of pre-registration or a registered report framework leaves open the possibility that the reported model was selected post-hoc from a broader analytic space.
issues.quote: A copy of the Mplus syntax used will be available on the NZAVS website upon acceptance of the manuscript.

issues.description: The central contribution of this paper is framed as advancing beyond Stanley et al.'s [14] student-sample longitudinal study by examining 'the general population.' This framing appears throughout the introduction, current study section, and discussion. However, the Methods describe a sample from an introductory psychology participant pool with M age=19—virtually identical in nature to a student sample. The discussion then explains the different pattern of results compared to Stanley et al. as due to 'sample type' (student vs. general population). If both samples are student pools, this explanation is invalid and the entire comparative narrative is undermined.
issues.quote: The present paper advances this research by examining the impact of SDO and RWA on environment-related attitudes in a general population sample, spanning five years... It is likely that the difference in sample type therefore accounts for the differences in our results, as we used a general population sample.

issues.description: A recurring theoretical tension in the paper is whether SDO predicts environmental exploitation because Social Dominants want dominance over nature itself, or because they use nature as a tool for dominance over other humans. The paper acknowledges this but does not resolve it. More critically, the SDO items used ('To get ahead in life, it is sometimes okay to step on other groups'; 'We should have increased social equality') frame hierarchy entirely in terms of human intergroup relations, not human-nature relations. Using these items to make conclusions about 'dominance over nature' is therefore conceptually unsupported by the operationalization. The measure cannot distinguish between the two competing mechanisms the paper discusses.
issues.quote: items in the SDO scale exclusively frame hierarchies based on intergroup relations... Milfont et al. [10] argue that Social Dominants' propensity for environmental exploitation exists 'because SDO promotes human hierarchical dominance over nature'

issues.description: The paper describes six items for SDO and six items for RWA, but the environmentalism measure's number of items is never stated—the Measures section describes only two example items and mentions it was 'modelled from' Liu and Sibley's scale. The total number of items constituting the WILL scale, whether all items are listed or a subset is shown, and how items were aggregated (mean, sum) are not reported. This prevents replication. Additionally, for RWA, with one item missing at Time 2, the effective number of items per time point (5 vs. 6) is not clarified, nor is whether scale scores were prorated.
issues.quote: Right-wing authoritarianism was assessed with six items from Altemeyer's [27] RWA scale... The item '...' was not assessed at time two, but included in all other time points.

issues.description: The Discussion draws broad conclusions about climate change motivation, SDO, and environmentalism as though findings apply universally. The paper cites IPCC reports, describes global climate change dynamics, and makes general statements about 'people' and 'humans' without consistently anchoring claims to the New Zealand context. Duckitt [3] is cited to explain that SDO and RWA may be particularly associated in New Zealand due to its polarized political system—this very fact makes NZ findings potentially non-generalizable to countries with different political structures. The implications sections (e.g., about framing climate change messages for high-SDO individuals) are presented as broadly applicable without qualification.
issues.quote: the motivation to exploit the environment comes primarily from the desire for dominance, and to a lesser extent from the desire to submit to tradition and authority.

issues.description: The Methods describe data collection across 'five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013).' The title describes a 'five-year' analysis. Five semesters spanning 2009–2013 would cover approximately 2.5 years (if consecutive semesters) or five years (if annual). The intervals between measurement points are not reported, yet they are directly relevant to interpreting the magnitude of cross-lagged effects. Cross-lagged effects of identical structural magnitude will produce different substantive interpretations depending on whether measurements are 6 months or 12 months apart. The term 'semesters' (implying ~6-month intervals) conflicts with the 'five-year' framing in the title.
issues.quote: This study uses data from individuals who participated across five semesters of the project (from 2009 to 2013).

issues.description: The lagged effect of willingness on RWA is reported as B = -.01, SE = .002, 95% CI [-.01, -.003]. With B = -.01 and SE = .002, the 95% CI should be approximately [-.014, -.006]. Reporting this as [-.01, -.003] is inconsistent: the lower bound (-.01) equals the point estimate, which is impossible for a symmetric interval, and the asymmetry (-.007 below vs. .007 above the point estimate) is not explained by the reported SE. Either the lower bound should be more negative or the upper bound is incorrectly truncated. This raises concern about rounding or transcription errors in the reporting of small-coefficient results.

The paper states 'We present standardized parameters, which vary across time points due to differences in observed variances,' yet the Results section and Figure 1 caption describe 'Unstandardized parameters.' This is a direct contradiction. Standardized and unstandardized coefficients serve different purposes (comparability vs. interpretability in original units), and it is unclear which set of parameters is actually reported. This ambiguity means the reported coefficients (e.g., B = -.11 for SDO) cannot be properly interpreted or compared across variables or studies.
issues.quote: We present standardized parameters, which vary across time points due to differences in observed variances. [...] Figure 1. Unstandardized parameters assessing the association between SDO, RWA, and willingness to sacrifice for the environment (WILL).

issues.description: The abstract states the study examines 'willingness to change their behaviour to benefit the environment,' and the current study section says 'willingness to change their behaviour to protect the environment.' The methods describe a measure of environmental concern and perceived exaggeration of environmental problems. The conclusion reports 'willingness to make sacrifices for the environment.' These inconsistencies across sections in describing the same outcome variable reflect either an imprecise manuscript or the use of a different scale than described—further reinforcing the construct validity concern about the mismatch between the described measure and the named outcome.
issues.quote: we examine how these ideological variables predict environmentalism across five time points... Environmentalism was measured as participants' concern about environmental problems.
